title: A New Radio to Overcome Critical Link Budgets

predicted_errors.error_location: Section IV.B.1, 'Rectangular Pulse Shape' (T = 18.375) and Eq. (3)/(4) definitions in Section III.A
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Earlier in the paper (Eq. 3 and surrounding text) T is defined as the dimension of a T×T matrix F_b and of the N×T transmit matrix T_b, i.e., a discrete number of time/sample slots used to build the FFT-like transmit structure. In the numeric example the paper sets 'T = 18.375', a non-integer value, which is incompatible with T being the size of a discrete matrix (number of time-domain samples/symbols). A transmit matrix cannot have a fractional number of columns, so this value violates the domain constraints established earlier in the derivation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section IV.B.1 ('Rectangular Pulse Shape', T=18.375, N=16) vs. Section on the N=32 example ('The combining gain is 15 dB, exactly the same as for transmit beamforming', T=46, N=32)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In the first numeric example the paper explicitly ties the combining gain to T, not N: 'Note that the temporal combining gain can exceed 12 dB as T = 18.375 > N = 16,' and the reported combining gain (12.6 dB) closely matches 10·log10(18.375) ≈ 12.64 dB (a T-fold gain), exceeding the N-fold beamforming gain of 10·log10(16) ≈ 12.0 dB. By the same logic, for the N=32 example where T=46 (T > N), the combining gain should exceed the N-fold beamforming gain of 10·log10(32) ≈ 15.05 dB and should approach 10·log10(46) ≈ 16.63 dB. Instead, the text states 'The combining gain is 15 dB, exactly the same as for transmit beamforming,' which contradicts the T-dependent relationship established by the first example.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ('MA-TISK does not require beam alignment') vs. Section IV.B ('a receiver employing analog beamforming towards the transmitter')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract advertises as a key advantage that, 'In contrast to common proposals that rely on analog beamforming at both transmitter and receiver, MA-TISK does not require beam alignment.' However, Section IV.B states the cost-effective receiver design 'is achieved by a receiver employing analog beamforming towards the transmitter,' which by definition requires directing/aligning a beam toward the transmitter. This directly undercuts the claimed benefit of avoiding beam alignment, since beam alignment is still required at the receiver side.
